doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Getting the RCA International job and creating the RCA label
summary: Through Dick Hadlock he joined RCA and helped build the catalogue of the new RCA label after the Victor trademark split.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well let me skip up a little bit, you worked as a producer for RCA and Atlantic?

Yeah. Let me see what happened. I got out of college and I played in a college band called the Red Onions and we used to play Jimmy Ryan’s on Monday nights alternating with Wilbur DeParis, where Omer Simeon played. I got to know Omer and he played an Albert system to hell. Hardly had any keys on it. It was like, I don’t know how he played. And so I got him a Buffet. Somebody gave me one and I gave it to him, or he gave me 20 bucks for it or something. I really wanted the horn myself but I couldn’t stand him, he was this great guy playing — and you know he was just so facile. He made that thing, the “Russian Rag” [scats] playing this thing on this primitive clarinet. So I loved him. His licks and everything, he was very influential on me. So that’s college. And I graduate, and I had a friend, also in part of this scene you know, the jam sessions and all that, a guy named Dick Hadlock. And Dick was on the west coast. He studied soprano with Bechet, with Sidney in Brooklyn. And Dick’s still got a radio program out there in San Francisco for years. Very nice guy. He wrote that book “Jazz Masters of the Twenties.” You know that? Dick is very knowledgeable. He knows almost as much as I do. I’m kidding of course. But he’s a grand guy. I love him. I mean he’s the sweetest, gentlest, knowledgeable. And he was working at RCA. And, at RCA International. And he wanted — they were going to expand the department and they were looking for somebody and they asked me was I interested. I said well I don’t know. I was going to be a music teacher but I student taught for two semesters and I hated it, I didn’t like it at all. So I got the job at RCA. And I enjoyed that very much, it was very good. It was very funny, there was a thing, it was RCA Victor, okay? That was the name of the American RCA company, they bought the — RCA bought Victor. When Sarnoff had the big hit with the radios in the late 20s or something they bought the Victor talking machine company and they became RCA Victor. And so their trademark, the dog and the phonograph and all that, and they had a deal with the English His Master’s Voice, the same trademark. You know France Le Vois DeMetre, you know, the same logo. And in those days the government was more efficient on such things, and I wonder why. But they were notified,

RCA, that it was a trust, a worldwide trust, you’re not allowed to have — one company controlling the whole world, you know, the competition. You’ve got to break it up. So Sarnoff decided, for legal reasons, they were going to create an RCA label and never mind the Victor and the dog and phonograph, to show that they really are competing against the English Victor talking machine, whatever. And so the RCA label was started. And Dick and I were in charge of that and we put together — it was great fun to put together a catalogue, you know, like what shall we have. We picked, you know, I succeeded, and Brian Rust said some little tale about it, but Benny Moten “South” was a record made in the 20s, and that was continually in RCA’s catalogue until the end of the 78 RPM era, ‘til ’45, an all-time best seller of some kind you know. So we made sure to put that in the catalogue, and all that kind of stuff. And it was just great fun you know, with the record business. Our boss was a guy named Frank McCall. And I got to talking with Frank McCall, he was a nice guy you know, smoking a cigar and pulling his hair out. And he used to work for Frank Walker in the 20s, and Frank Walker was the recording director at Columbia Records and he recorded Bessie Smith. And he told me this marvelous story about that Bessie was trying to suck up to Frank Walker and came in one day in Philadelphia with a bicycle and that still had the price on it, and she gave it to him to give to his daughter.
